title: Given two strings, return the length of the longest substring (contiguous) that appears in both.
shortTitle: Longest Common Substring — contiguous match 2D DP

s1_definition.profdef: 2D DP where dp[i][j] is the length of the common substring ending exactly at A[i−1] and B[j−1]. If they match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]+1; if not, dp[i][j] = 0 (the run breaks). Track the global maximum cell. Time O(m·n), space O(m·n) or O(n) rolling.
s1_definition.analogy: A log-forensics tool at National Bank of India compares two server logs to find the longest identical contiguous block, maybe a replayed request. When the current characters match the shared run grows by one; the instant they differ the run resets to zero.
s1_definition.oneliner: Match ⇒ diagonal+1; mismatch ⇒ 0; answer is the biggest cell, not the corner.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 2D DP where dp[i][j] is the length of the common substring ending exactly at A[i−1] and B[j−1]. If they match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]+1; if not, dp[i][j] = 0 (the run breaks). Track the global maximum cell. Time O(m·n), space O(m·n) or O(n) rolling.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A log-forensics tool at National Bank of India compares two server logs to find the longest identical contiguous block, maybe a replayed request. When the current characters match the shared run grows by one; the instant they differ the run resets to zero.

**One line to remember:** Match ⇒ diagonal+1; mismatch ⇒ 0; answer is the biggest cell, not the corner.

sections.s2_technical:
This looks like Longest Common Subsequence but differs crucially because a substring must be contiguous. So dp[i][j] means the length of the common run ending exactly at those two positions, not the best up to here. When the characters match, extend the diagonal: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]+1. For example: `if (a.charAt(i-1)==b.charAt(j-1)) dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]+1;`.

When they differ the run is broken, so dp[i][j] resets to zero rather than inheriting a neighbor. Because the answer is not necessarily at the bottom-right corner, you track a running maximum over all cells as you fill them.

The time and space are O(m·n), reducible to O(n) with a rolling row. A senior nuance is that the only structural differences from LCS are the reset to zero on mismatch and taking the global maximum instead of the corner, which is a common interview trap when people conflate substring with subsequence.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a forensics tool compares two server request logs to find the longest identical contiguous block, which may indicate a replayed or duplicated request. This is exactly how Longest Common Substring works.

Problem 2 — A replay must be a contiguous identical run, so skipping characters as in subsequence matching would give false positives. This is exactly why the run resets to zero on any mismatch.

The mini-project builds a `LogForensics`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input strings are ABABC and BABCA.

Step 1: The table starts with a zero border for empty prefixes.

Step 2: Matching characters extend the diagonal run, so where BABC lines up the cells climb one, two, three, four.

Step 3: Any mismatched cell resets to zero, breaking the current run immediately.

Step 4: The running maximum captures the longest run of four as it is produced, not at the corner.

Step 5: The answer is four for the shared BABC, and abc versus xyz has no match so it is zero.

```text
2026-10-27T03:50:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Log Forensics (Longest Common Substring)
2026-10-27T03:50:00Z [INFO] Longest common substring length = 4
2026-10-27T03:50:00Z [INFO] 'ABABC' vs 'BABCA' → 4
2026-10-27T03:50:00Z [INFO] Longest common substring length = 0
2026-10-27T03:50:00Z [INFO] 'abc' vs 'xyz' → 0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Common Substring looks almost identical to Longest Common Subsequence but differs in two important ways because a substring must be contiguous. I define dp of i and j as the length of the common run that ends exactly at those two positions, not the best up to here. When the current characters match, I extend the diagonal by one, building a contiguous run.

The two differences from the subsequence version are the heart of the problem. First, when the characters differ, the run is broken, so the cell resets to zero rather than inheriting from a neighbor. Second, because the longest run can end anywhere, the answer is the global maximum over all cells, not the bottom-right corner. Conflating these with the subsequence version is a classic trap.

In my project at National Bank of India, a forensics tool compared two server request logs to find the longest identical contiguous block that might indicate a replayed request. Because a replay must be a contiguous identical run, I used this substring DP that resets to zero on any mismatch and tracks the global maximum cell, and I can reduce it to a rolling row for memory.
